To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
a wearable device capable of detecting both types of seizures can be developed using a combination of heart rate, arterial blood oxygenation and electro-dermal activity.
we have developed a three stage methodology for detecting seizures in patients with epilepsy that has been tested on 10 patients in a clinical setting.

1) seizures can be detected with high sensitivity by a wearable device that monitors three physiological signals (ECG, SpO2 and GSR) in the presence of a high level of motion; 2) seizures can be distinguished from nonseizures using a combination of these three signals; 3) the seizure detection rate is improved by the use of EEG signals.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the design of a wearable device for seizure detection.
the development of a wearable seizure detection device for patients with epilepsy.
developing a seizure detection system that can be worn by patients in everyday life and that can detect seizures that may not be detectable by a single biosignal.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
our methodology is capable of detecting all seizures in patients who have a high percentage of seizures that are detected in Stage II.
our methodology has detected all seizures from seven out of 10 patients and that it is capable of detecting seizures from all patients with appropriate modifications to the system.
Stage I is capable of detecting all seizures in all patients, but that Stage II is more sensitive to seizures than Stage I and that Stage III is capable of detecting seizures in some patients.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the three stages of our seizure detection algorithm are effective in detecting seizures of patients with different types of epilepsies.
our methodology is capable of detecting seizures with a low false positive rate, and that our methodology is able to detect all seizures in the majority of the patients we studied.
we have demonstrated a methodology for seizure detection in a clinical setting that is capable of detecting both nonconvulsive and convulsive seizures.
The main takeaway from our work is that
it is possible to develop a wearable device that can detect both convulsive and some nonconvulsive seizures with a very low false alarm rate.
the combination of multiple biosignals, especially those that can be measured by wrist-worn devices, can provide a robust seizure detection methodology.
the combination of Stage I with either Stage II or III can detect all seizures from a patient.
